control_ladder.note_beginner: On a nasturtium you are keeping for its flowers and leaves, a firm stream from the hose lifts the clusters off the stems and new growth. Aphids finding this plant is normal rather than a sign that something has gone wrong, so aim for a planting you are happy to look at instead of an empty one, and go again when fresh clusters appear.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Heavy aphid interest here is the expected condition rather than a failure, so read a hose-down of colonized stems and new growth as periodic knock-back on a planting you intend to keep, not as a push toward zero. Spray early in the day so foliage dries, and plan to repeat as the plant pushes fresh growth.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The flowers pull in ladybugs and hoverflies, helpful insects whose young eat aphids, and on nasturtium they usually hold the numbers down to something you can live with. Give them room to work, and skip broad insect sprays that would take them out along with the aphids.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conservation carries most of the load: the hoverflies, lacewings, and ladybugs the blooms recruit generally keep colonies in check on a planting you are keeping. Withholding broad-spectrum materials is what preserves that pressure, and it counts for more on a plant that concentrates aphids than on one that rarely carries them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If clusters keep building on a planting you want to keep looking good, coat them with insecticidal soap, a mild soap-based spray that acts only on what it actually wets. Treat just the loaded stems so the ladybugs and hoverflies working the rest of the plant come through it, and hold off during a hot spell or on a plant that is dry and stressed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is the last step the guidance offers here, for colonies the resident predators have not held on a planting you mean to keep. It acts by contact, so coverage of the loaded stems and shoot tips decides the result; spot-treat rather than blanket a plant whose flowers are feeding those predators, and keep it off water-stressed growth and out of hot weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where it is practical, lay a floating row cover, a thin fabric sheet that passes light and rain while shutting insects out, over the planting so the white butterflies cannot reach the leaves to lay eggs. Eggs they cannot lay are caterpillars you do not have to find later. This is easier over a young or contained planting than over one that has run out across the bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Exclusion heads off egg-laying instead of treating larvae, and the butterfly is here for a reason: nasturtium shares the mustard-oil chemistry that its brassica hosts carry. The guidance qualifies the cover as practical-where-possible, which on a plant that sprawls into a low mat generally means the early weeks rather than the whole season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Check the leaves and pick the green caterpillars off by hand. On nasturtium the chewed holes are a looks problem rather than a threat to the plant, so a regular pass is usually as much control as the leaves need.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hand removal is the working control at garden scale, and the tolerance is generous: this feeding is cosmetic on nasturtium, so the object is keeping leaves usable rather than clearing the planting. Pick on a routine walk rather than waiting for damage to accumulate.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For an outbreak that gets bad, Bt is a natural spray made from a soil bacterium that upsets a caterpillar's gut and leaves most other insects alone. Keep it to the nasturtiums that actually have caterpillars on them, since it does not sort a cabbage white's young from a swallowtail's, and put it on again after rain.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) is where the guidance sends heavy pressure, and it does its best work on small larvae before much leaf has gone. It degrades in the field, so plan on repeat coverage after rain and across new growth, and confine applications to the affected planting: this material takes caterpillars as a group, desirable species included.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put a light row cover over young nasturtiums, meaning a thin fabric sheet laid across them that passes light and rain but stops the hopping beetles from landing. Once a plant is established the small round holes are mostly a looks problem, so this is an early-season job rather than something you keep up all summer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cover young plantings, the stage the guidance singles out; on an established plant the shot-hole pitting stays cosmetic, so exclusion is an establishment tool rather than a standing program. Expect beetle interest here in any case, since nasturtium is among the plants they favor, and judge the cover by whether seedlings are being set back rather than by how many holes you can count.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Take away the damp daytime shelters near the planting: heavy mulch, boards, and old plant debris. Nasturtium makes this harder than most plants, because the trailing mat it grows into is itself good cover, so thin the mulch around it rather than adding more.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reducing mulch and debris strips out the harborage you can actually control. A vigorous nasturtium sprawls into a mat that shelters them on its own, so work the surroundings, and expect feeding to concentrate on seedlings and the low foliage through damp spells.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go out after dark with a flashlight and pick them off. They feed at night in damp weather, and tender nasturtium seedlings are one of the first things they go for, so the nights just after sowing or planting out are the ones worth walking.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Night handpicking in damp conditions removes the feeders directly, and the passes that pay best cover seedlings, which the guidance names as a favored target. Work the low, sprawling growth as well, where the ragged feeding accumulates out of sight.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where the ragged holes keep appearing despite the cleanup and the night rounds, iron phosphate bait is the lower-risk pellet to fall back on. Scatter it on the soil around the plants rather than on the foliage, and use the rate the label gives.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Iron phosphate bait backs up the harborage work and the night rounds when damp weather keeps pressure on. Place it on the soil surface rather than in the canopy and keep to the label; a lower-risk bait is still a pesticide, and the leaves and flowers on this plant go to the kitchen.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hose the foliage, aiming up under the leaves where both of these sit. The whiteflies rise in a cloud when you disturb them, and the mites show as fine speckling in hot, dry spells. A rinse knocks numbers back, and outdoors that is usually as far as you need to go.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Direct the spray at leaf undersides, the surface both colonize, and go back over it as you scout rather than treating a single pass as the job. Both stay secondary problems on nasturtium outdoors, so the rinse is maintenance on stressed or sheltered plants rather than the opening of a program.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If they keep building, insecticidal soap, a mild soap-based spray that works only where it wets the pest, is the next step. Coat the undersides of the leaves, and skip it during a hot spell or on a plant that is already dry and stressed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is the material the guidance holds back for a persistent infestation. It acts on contact, so underside coverage is the whole job and successive hatches mean repeat passes; keep it on the growth actually carrying the pest, and avoid applying in heat or to water-stressed plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Nothing cures a plant once a virus is inside it, so pull the ones whose leaves are badly mottled, streaked, or twisted and bag them for the trash instead of the compost. Taking them out early leaves the aphids less to pick the virus up from as they move through the planting.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Roguing is the whole of what is available: with no treatment, a symptomatic plant is a standing source that aphid vectors acquire from and carry onward. Remove plants showing mosaic mottling, ringspots, or distortion promptly and destroy them, and read the aphid load this plant carries as part of the same picture, since those insects are what move these viruses.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a nasturtium suddenly droops and collapses, do not put another one back in the same spot. This wilt lives in the soil, so shifting the next planting to different ground, a habit gardeners call crop rotation, is the step that does the work. It is mostly a hot, humid-region problem.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The bacterium is soilborne, so the site carries the risk forward and moving the planting beats anything you could apply to it. Weight this by geography: the collapse is most relevant in the warm, humid Deep South, and the guidance calls it uncommon outside those conditions, so the rotation is a regional priority rather than a universal one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A plant that has wilted with this will not recover, and no spray changes that, so lift it out and put it in the trash rather than the compost. Getting the collapsed tissue out of the bed keeps it from carrying the problem into whatever you plant next.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removal is containment, not rescue: there is no chemical control, so the collapsed plant comes out and is destroyed rather than buried or composted, since diseased tissue can carry a soilborne organism forward. It pairs with keeping the following planting off that ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Nothing brings an infected plant back, so the useful move is a quick one: take out any nasturtium with yellowed, twisted growth or blooms coming out green, roots included, and bag it rather than composting it. A plant left standing is what the leafhoppers move the disease from.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt roguing is the entire response available. A phytoplasma is delivered by leafhoppers as they feed, so nothing applied to the plant reaches it, and every symptomatic plant left in place is material a vector can acquire and pass on. Nasturtium carries few diseases overall, so this is an occasional find rather than a standing worry.
